stem: You run `node --watch main.cjs`. `main.cjs` does `require('./dep.cjs')` and reads `data.txt` with `fs.readFileSync`. Which edit makes Node restart the script?

options.text: Editing `data.txt`, because watch mode follows every file the process opens
options.why: Watch mode tracks the module graph, not files read with `fs`. Editing `data.txt` does nothing.

options.text: Editing `dep.cjs`, because watch mode tracks the entry file and the modules it loads
options.why: Node watches the entry point plus every module it `require`s or `import`s.

options.text: Editing any file in the working directory, because `--watch` watches the current folder
options.why: That describes nodemon's default, not Node's built-in watch mode.

options.text: None of them until you pass `--watch-path`, because `--watch` alone only prints a notice
options.why: `--watch` restarts on its own; `--watch-path` only changes what is watched.

explanation: Built-in watch mode (stable since Node 22) restarts the process when the entry file or any module in its dependency graph changes. Data files read with `fs` are not part of that graph, so editing them never triggers a restart; add them with `--watch-path` if you need that. Verified on Node 24: editing `data.txt` and an unrelated file caused no restart, while editing `dep.cjs` did.

stem: A service is started with `node --watch-path=./config main.cjs`, and `main.cjs` requires `./dep.cjs`. A developer edits `dep.cjs`, then edits `config/app.json`. How many times does the process restart?

options.text: Twice, because `--watch-path` adds `./config` on top of the module graph that watch mode already tracks
options.why: It does not add to the module graph: it replaces it.

options.text: Once, after `config/app.json` changes: `--watch-path` turns off watching of loaded modules
options.why: Only the listed paths are watched, so the `dep.cjs` edit is ignored.

options.text: Never, because `--watch-path` only works when `--watch` is also passed
options.why: `--watch-path` starts watch mode by itself.

options.text: Once, after `dep.cjs` changes, because JSON files are never watched
options.why: Any file under a watched path triggers a restart, including JSON.

explanation: Per the Node.js CLI docs, `--watch-path` starts watch mode and watches only the given paths, turning off watching of required or imported modules even if `--watch` is also passed. So the `dep.cjs` edit is ignored and the `config/app.json` edit restarts the process. Verified on Node 24. To watch both, list every path you need, for example `--watch-path=./src --watch-path=./config`.

stem: Which Node.js command-line flag restarts your script automatically when it or a module it imports changes, without installing nodemon? Type the flag.
explanation: `node --watch app.js` is built-in watch mode, stable since Node 22. It restarts the process when the entry file or its imported modules change, and clears the console on restart unless you pass `--watch-preserve-output`. Tools like nodemon are now optional for this simple case.

stem: A test calls `assert.strictEqual(1, '1')` from `node:assert` and catches the error as `err`. Which statement is true?

options.text: `err` is a `TypeError`, because the two values have different types
options.why: Assertion failures are always `AssertionError`, whatever the values.

options.text: `err.code` is `'ERR_ASSERTION'` and `err.actual` holds the number `1`
options.why: AssertionError exposes `actual`, `expected`, `operator` and the code `ERR_ASSERTION`.

options.text: `err.expected` holds the number `1`, because both sides are coerced first
options.why: `strictEqual` never coerces; `expected` is the string `'1'`.

options.text: `err.operator` is `'==='`, the JavaScript operator that was used
options.why: `operator` names the assertion method: `'strictEqual'`.

explanation: A failed assertion throws `assert.AssertionError` with `name` `'AssertionError'`, `code` `'ERR_ASSERTION'`, and the fields `actual` (1), `expected` (`'1'`) and `operator` (`'strictEqual'`). Test runners read these fields to show diffs. `generatedMessage` is `true` because no custom message was passed. Verified on Node 24.

options.text: It copies the current stack into `e.cause` so the original error is preserved
options.why: `captureStackTrace` sets `e.stack`; it never touches `cause`.

options.text: It rebuilds `e.stack` so the frames start at the code that called `httpError`
options.why: Frames above and including the given function are left out of the trace.

options.text: It stops V8 from collecting a stack at all, which makes the factory faster
options.why: It still captures a stack, just starting from a different frame.

options.text: It turns the error into an `AssertionError` so test runners print a diff
options.why: The class and name stay the same; only the stack text changes.

explanation: `Error.captureStackTrace(targetObject, constructorOpt)` writes a fresh `stack` to the target, omitting `constructorOpt` and every frame above it. Helpers and custom error classes use it so the trace points at the real call site instead of the helper. Verified on Node 24: without it the top frame was the factory; with it the top frame was the caller.

options.text: It passes, because any thrown error satisfies `assert.throws`
options.why: The second argument is a validation: the error must be a `RangeError`.

options.text: The original `TypeError` propagates out unchanged
options.why: Node wraps the mismatch in an assertion failure instead of rethrowing as is.

options.text: It throws an `AssertionError` saying a `RangeError` was expected but a `TypeError` was received
options.why: A thrown error that fails the class check becomes an assertion failure.

options.text: It throws a `TypeError` of its own, because an error class is not a valid second argument for `assert.throws`
options.why: Passing an error class is one of the documented validation forms.

explanation: When the function throws but the error fails the validation (a class, regular expression, object or function), `assert.throws` fails with an `AssertionError`. In Node 24 the message reads: The error is expected to be an instance of "RangeError". Received "TypeError", followed by the original message. That makes it easy to spot a test that only passes because the wrong error is thrown.

options.text: `ValidationError ValidationError: bad email`
options.why: `name` is inherited from `Error.prototype` unless you set it yourself.

options.text: `Error Error: bad email`
options.why: The subclass inherits `name = 'Error'`, so logs show the generic name.

options.text: `undefined Error: bad email`
options.why: `name` is defined on `Error.prototype`, so it is never undefined.

options.text: `ValidationError bad email`
options.why: `String(err)` always uses the `name: message` format.

explanation: Extending `Error` does not change `name`; it is still the inherited `Error.prototype.name`, which is `'Error'`. Logs, `String(err)` and the first line of `err.stack` therefore all say `Error: bad email`. Set it in the constructor (`this.name = 'ValidationError'`) or as a class field. Branching on `err instanceof ValidationError` works either way. Verified on Node 24.

stem: A logger writes structured logs with `JSON.stringify({ msg: 'charge failed', err })`, where `err` is an `Error` with a custom `this.name = 'PaymentError'` and a `cause`. What appears under `err` in the log line?

options.text: The name, message and stack, because `Error` defines a `toJSON` method
options.why: `Error` has no `toJSON`; only enumerable own properties are serialised.

options.text: Only `{"name":"PaymentError"}`: `message`, `stack` and `cause` are non-enumerable
options.why: The assigned `name` is enumerable; the built-in fields are not.

options.text: An empty object, because `JSON.stringify` skips every property of an `Error`, including ones you set
options.why: Properties you assign yourself, like `name`, are enumerable and are kept.

options.text: The message only, because `JSON.stringify` calls `String(err)` for errors
options.why: It serialises objects by their enumerable own properties, not by `toString`.

explanation: `message`, `stack` and `cause` are created as non-enumerable own properties, so `JSON.stringify` drops them, and a plain `new Error('x')` serialises to `{}`. Assigning `this.name` creates an enumerable property, so it alone survives. Use the logger's error serializer (for example pino's `err` serializer) or copy the fields explicitly. Verified on Node 24.

stem: `fs.readFileSync('missing.txt')` throws because the file does not exist. Which two statements about the thrown error are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: `err.code` is `'ENOENT'`, the portable way to branch on the failure
options.why: System errors carry the POSIX-style code as a string.

options.text: `err.syscall` is `'open'` and `err.path` holds the path that failed
options.why: System errors record the failing system call and its arguments.

options.text: `err.errno` is always `-2`, so you can compare it on every platform
options.why: `errno` is platform-specific (for example -4058 on Windows), so compare `code`.

options.text: `err.name` is `'SystemError'`, a dedicated error class
options.why: The object is an ordinary `Error`; `name` is `'Error'`.

options.text: The error is only reported through `process.on('error')`
options.why: Synchronous fs calls throw directly, so `try`/`catch` handles them.

explanation: Node's system errors are `Error` objects with extra fields: `code` (such as `ENOENT`, `EACCES`, `EADDRINUSE`), `syscall`, `path`, and a numeric `errno` whose value differs between platforms. Branch on `code`, never on `errno` or the message text. Verified on Node 24 on Windows: `ENOENT`, `open`, and `errno` -4058.

stem: A CLI is run as `node app.js deploy --dry-run`. What is `process.argv[2]`?

options.text: `'app.js'`
options.why: Index 1 holds the script path; index 2 is the first user argument.

options.text: `'deploy'`
options.why: Index 0 is the node binary, 1 the script, and user arguments start at 2.

options.text: `'--dry-run'`
options.why: That is the second user argument, at index 3.

options.text: `'node'`
options.why: The executable path is at index 0, not 2.

explanation: `process.argv[0]` is the absolute path of the Node executable, `process.argv[1]` the absolute path of the script, and user arguments start at index 2, which is why CLIs use `process.argv.slice(2)` or `util.parseArgs()`. Verified on Node 24.

stem:
What does this print?

```bash
node -e "console.log(process.argv.slice(1))" a b
```

options.why: Node consumes its own flags; they never appear in `process.argv`.
With `-e` there is no script path, so user arguments start at index 1.
`[eval]` is the module name used in stack traces, not an argv entry.
Every trailing argument is passed through, not just the first.

explanation: With a script file, `process.argv[1]` is the script path. With `-e` or `-p` there is no file, so the first user argument lands at index 1, and code that blindly does `slice(2)` loses it. Prefer `util.parseArgs()`, which reads arguments correctly in both cases. Verified on Node 24.

stem: A script must read all of its piped input, as in `cat data.csv | node import.js`. Which code reads the whole input correctly?

options.text: `const data = process.stdin.read();` at the top of the script
options.why: At startup nothing has been buffered yet, so `read()` returns `null`.

options.text: `let s = ''; for await (const chunk of process.stdin) s += chunk;`
options.why: The loop collects every chunk and ends when the input stream closes.

options.text: `process.stdin.on('data', (c) => { parse(c); });`, parsing each chunk
options.why: A chunk can end mid-line, so parsing chunks separately breaks records.

options.text: `const data = require('fs').readFileSync(process.stdin.fd);` after checking `isTTY`
options.why: Reading the descriptor synchronously can fail on pipes on some platforms; the stream API is the portable choice.

explanation: `process.stdin` is a Readable stream, so `for await` collects every chunk until end of input, and the joined text can then be parsed safely. Chunk boundaries are arbitrary, so per-chunk parsing splits lines; use `readline` if you want line by line. `process.stdin.isTTY` is `undefined` when input is piped, which is how a CLI tells piped input from an interactive terminal. Verified on Node 24.

stem: A package declares `"bin": { "mkreport": "./cli.js" }`, and `cli.js` starts with `#!/usr/bin/env node`. After `npm install mkreport` in a project, typing `mkreport` in the shell prints "command not found". Why, and what is the usual fix?

options.text: The shebang is wrong; it must be `#!/usr/bin/node` or npm ignores the file
options.why: `/usr/bin/env node` is the recommended, portable shebang.

options.text: Local bins go to `node_modules/.bin`, which isn't on the PATH; use `npx mkreport` or a script
options.why: npm scripts and npx add `node_modules/.bin` to the PATH for you.

options.text: The `bin` field only works for packages published under a scope such as `@acme/`, not plain names
options.why: Scoped and unscoped packages both support `bin`.

options.text: npm needs `"type": "module"` before it can link any executable
options.why: The module type is unrelated to how npm links executables.

explanation: npm links each `bin` entry into the project's `node_modules/.bin` (with `.cmd` shims on Windows). That folder is not on your shell's PATH, but `npm run` scripts and `npx` add it, so `npx mkreport` or a `"scripts"` entry works. A global install (`npm i -g`) links into a folder that is on the PATH. The shebang tells Unix shells to run the file with Node.
reference: npm docs: package.json bin; npm docs: folders

stem: `package.json` defines `"prebuild": "node tools/gen.js"` and `"build": "node tools/build.js"`. What is the difference between `npm run build` and `node --run build` (Node 22+)?

options.text: None: `node --run` is an alias that launches npm under the hood
options.why: `node --run` runs the script itself without starting npm.

options.text: `npm run build` runs `prebuild` first; `node --run build` runs only `build`
options.why: `node --run` deliberately skips pre and post scripts to stay fast and simple.

options.text: `node --run build` runs `prebuild` and `build` in parallel
options.why: It never runs `prebuild` at all.

options.text: `node --run` only works for scripts whose command starts with `node`, not other shell commands
options.why: It runs any shell command in the script, like npm does.

explanation: `node --run <script>` executes a `package.json` script directly, adding `node_modules/.bin` to the PATH, and starts much faster than npm. To stay small it does not run `pre`/`post` lifecycle scripts. Verified on Node 24: `npm run build` printed the prebuild output and then build; `node --run build` printed only build. Extra arguments go after `--` with both commands.

stem: `package.json` has `pretest`, `test` and `posttest` scripts, and you run `npm test`. Put what npm runs in order.

options.text: `pretest`
`test`
`posttest`

explanation: For any script `x`, npm runs `prex`, then `x`, then `postx`, stopping if one exits non-zero. So a failing `test` means `posttest` never runs. The same applies to `npm run build` with `prebuild` and `postbuild`. `node --run` skips the pre and post scripts. Verified with npm 11 on Node 24.
reference: npm docs: scripts (pre and post scripts)

stem: A repo has `"workspaces": ["packages/*"]` in the root `package.json`, with `packages/util` (named `@acme/util`) and `packages/app`, which depends on `@acme/util`. After `npm install` at the root, how does `require('@acme/util')` in `packages/app` resolve?

options.text: npm downloads `@acme/util` from the registry into `packages/app/node_modules`
options.why: Matching workspaces are linked locally, not fetched from the registry.

options.text: Through a symlink at the root `node_modules/@acme/util` pointing to `packages/util`
options.why: Edits in `packages/util` show up immediately, with no publish or reinstall.

options.text: Through a copy of `packages/util` that npm makes during install and refreshes on `npm run build`
options.why: npm creates a link, not a copy, so there is nothing to refresh.

options.text: It fails until `packages/util` is published, because workspaces only share scripts
options.why: Workspaces exist so that local packages can depend on each other.

explanation: npm workspaces link each workspace package into the root `node_modules` (a symlink, or a junction on Windows). Node's resolver walks up from `packages/app`, finds the root `node_modules/@acme/util`, and follows the link to `packages/util`. The lockfile records it as `{"resolved": "packages/util", "link": true}`. Verified with npm 11 on Node 24.

stem: In an npm workspaces monorepo the root `package.json` has no `build` or `lint` script, `packages/app` and `packages/util` both define `build`, and only `packages/util` defines `lint`. Which two commands, run at the root, succeed? (Choose two.)

options.text: `npm run build -w app`, which runs `build` only in the `app` workspace
options.why: `-w` (or `--workspace`) targets one workspace by name or path.

options.text: `npm run lint --workspaces --if-present`, which skips workspaces without `lint`
options.why: `--if-present` turns a missing script into a no-op instead of an error.

options.text: `npm run build`, which runs `build` in every workspace automatically
options.why: Without `-w` or `--workspaces` npm looks only at the root, and the root has no `build`.

options.text: `npm run lint --workspaces`, which skips `app` because it has no `lint`
options.why: Without `--if-present` it fails with "Missing script" in `app`.

options.text: `npm run build --workspace=util`, using the folder name instead of the package name
options.why: The package is named `@acme/util`; use that name or the path `packages/util`.

explanation: Workspace flags select where a script runs: `-w <name|path>` for one workspace, `--workspaces` for all. A missing script is an error in every selected workspace unless you add `--if-present`. Plain `npm run build` at the root runs only the root's scripts and fails with "Missing script". Verified with npm 11 (`build -w app`, `--if-present`, and the two failures).

stem: `package.json` lists `"express": "^4.18.0"`. The installed version is 4.18.2, the newest 4.x is 4.21.2, and 5.1.0 is tagged `latest`. What does `npm update express` do with npm 10?

options.text: Installs 5.1.0 and rewrites the range to `^5.1.0`
options.why: `npm update` never crosses the range in `package.json`; a major bump needs `npm install express@5`.

options.text: Installs 4.21.2 and updates the lockfile, leaving the range in `package.json` unchanged
options.why: It moves to the highest version that satisfies `^4.18.0` and only saves ranges with `--save`.

options.text: Nothing, because a caret range locks the exact version already installed
options.why: `^4.18.0` allows any 4.x at or above 4.18.0.

options.text: Installs 4.21.2 and also rewrites the range to `^4.21.2` in `package.json` to match the lockfile
options.why: npm 8 and later don't touch `package.json` ranges unless you pass `--save`.

explanation: `npm update` installs the newest version that satisfies each declared range and records it in `package-lock.json`. By default (npm 8+) it leaves the semver ranges in `package.json` alone; `npm update --save` also bumps them. Moving to a new major is a deliberate `npm install pkg@5`. `npm outdated` shows this as Current 4.18.2, Wanted 4.21.2, Latest 5.1.0.
reference: npm docs: npm update; npm outdated

stem: Match each `npm outdated` column with what it shows.

options.text: The version installed in `node_modules` now
The highest version that satisfies the range in `package.json`
The version tagged `latest` in the registry

explanation: `npm outdated` compares three versions per dependency. Current is what is installed. Wanted is the newest version your declared range allows, which is what `npm update` would install. Latest is the registry's `latest` tag, which may be a new major outside your range. Red rows mean Wanted is above Current; yellow means Latest is above your range.

stem: A developer runs `npm install -g eslint`. `eslint` now works in the terminal, but `require('eslint')` inside a project fails with `MODULE_NOT_FOUND`. Why?

options.text: Global packages need `"type": "module"` before they can be required
options.why: The module type has nothing to do with where Node looks for packages.

options.text: Global installs go to npm's global prefix, which isn't on the module resolution path
options.why: Node searches `node_modules` folders above the requiring file, not the global prefix.

options.text: npm installs only the executable globally and throws away the package's library code
options.why: The full package is installed in the global `node_modules`; Node just doesn't look there.

options.text: The project's lockfile blocks every package it doesn't list
options.why: Lockfiles drive installs, not runtime resolution.

explanation: Global installs land in `{prefix}/lib/node_modules` (or `%AppData%\npm\node_modules` on Windows), and their bins are linked into a folder on your PATH. Node's resolver only walks up the `node_modules` folders above the requiring file, so the global copy is invisible to `require`. Install libraries locally (`npm i -D eslint`) and keep globals for standalone CLIs, or use `npx`. `npm root -g` shows the global folder.
reference: npm docs: folders; Node.js docs: modules (loading from node_modules)

stem: A build script uses `fs.globSync('src/**/*.js')` (Node 22+) and then checks `files.includes('src/a/y.js')`. It passes in CI on Linux but fails on a Windows laptop even though the file exists. Why?

options.text: `fs.globSync` is not supported on Windows, so it silently returns an empty array there
options.why: It works on Windows; it just returns native paths.

options.text: It returns paths with the platform separator, such as `src\a\y.js` on Windows
options.why: Compare with `path.join(...)` or normalise the results before matching.

options.text: `**` matches only one directory level on Windows
options.why: The globstar matches any depth on every platform.

options.text: Windows paths are case-insensitive, so the results are upper-cased
options.why: Case is preserved; the difference is the separator.

explanation: `fs.glob`/`fs.globSync` return paths built with the platform's separator, so on Windows the result is `src\a\y.js`. Comparing against a hard-coded forward-slash string breaks there. Build expected paths with `path.join`, or normalise results (for example `p.split(path.sep).join('/')`). Verified on Node 24 on Windows: `["src\\a\\y.js","src\\x.js"]`.

options.text: `{ debug: true } true`
options.why: Top-level `var` in a browser script becomes a global, but Node modules have their own scope.

options.text: `undefined true`
options.why: The module wrapper keeps `config` local, and `global` is an alias of `globalThis`.

options.text: `undefined false`
options.why: `global` and `globalThis` are the same object in Node.

options.text: A `ReferenceError`, because `global` is not defined in CommonJS
options.why: `global` exists in every Node module type.

explanation: Node wraps each CommonJS module in a function, and ES modules have their own scope too, so top-level `var`, `let` and `function` declarations never become properties of the global object. Only explicit assignments such as `globalThis.config = ...` do. In Node, `global` is a legacy alias for `globalThis`. Verified on Node 24.
reference: Node.js docs: Globals; Modules (the module wrapper)

stem: A shared library detects the browser with `const isBrowser = typeof navigator !== 'undefined';` and then touches `window.localStorage`. After the team moves its server from Node 18 to Node 22, server rendering crashes with `ReferenceError: window is not defined`. Why?

options.text: Node 22 removed the `global` object, so every `typeof` check now returns `'object'`
options.why: `global` still exists, and `typeof` checks behave as before.

options.text: Node 21+ defines a global `navigator`, so the check now treats Node as a browser
options.why: `navigator.userAgent` is `Node.js/22` in Node; test for `window` or `document` instead.

options.text: Node 22 started setting `window` during server rendering, then deletes it
options.why: Node has never defined `window`; that is exactly why the code crashes.

options.text: The bundler replaced `navigator` with `undefined` only in production builds
options.why: The crash comes from the runtime, not from a bundler substitution.

explanation: Node 21 added a browser-compatible global `navigator` (with `hardwareConcurrency`, `language`, `platform` and `userAgent`), so `typeof navigator` is `'object'` on the server and the detection misfires. Feature-detect what you actually use (`typeof window !== 'undefined'` or `typeof document`), or check `process.versions?.node`. Verified on Node 24: `typeof navigator` is `object` and `navigator.userAgent` is `Node.js/24`.

stem: A team adds OpenTelemetry auto-instrumentation by calling `sdk.start()` in `tracing.js`, which `app.js` requires after `const express = require('express')`. Traces show outgoing HTTP calls but no Express route spans. What is the fix?

options.text: Switch to the `diagnostics_channel` API instead, because Express has no OpenTelemetry instrumentation
options.why: Express spans come from the OpenTelemetry Express instrumentation once it loads first.

options.text: Load the instrumentation before any app code, for example `node --require ./tracing.js app.js`
options.why: Instrumentations patch modules as they load, so Express must load after them.

options.text: Call `sdk.start()` inside every route handler so each request gets a span
options.why: Starting the SDK repeatedly doesn't patch modules that were already loaded.

options.text: Increase the sampling rate, because route spans are sampled out by default
options.why: Sampling drops whole traces; it can't remove only the Express spans.

explanation: OpenTelemetry's Node auto-instrumentations work by hooking `require`/`import` and patching libraries as they load. If `express` was required before the SDK started, it is already loaded unpatched, so no route spans appear, while `http` (patched differently) may still show up. Start the SDK first with a preload: `node --require ./tracing.js app.js` for CommonJS, or `node --import ./tracing.mjs app.mjs` for ES modules.
reference: OpenTelemetry docs: Node.js getting started (instrumentation setup)

stem:
An Express app renders profiles with EJS, using `

<%- user.bio %>

`. A user saves a bio containing ``, and it runs in other visitors' browsers. What is the fix?

options.text: Switch to `res.send()` instead of `res.render()`, which escapes HTML
options.why: `res.send` sends the string as is; it escapes nothing.

options.text: Use `<%= user.bio %>`, which HTML-escapes the value before output
options.why: `<%-` writes raw HTML; `<%=` escapes it.

options.text: Strip `<script>` tags from the bio with a regular expression before saving
options.why: Regex filtering misses event handlers and other payloads; escape on output instead.

options.text: Set `app.set('view cache', true)` so templates are compiled safely
options.why: View caching only affects performance, not escaping.

explanation: EJS has two output tags: `<%= value %>` escapes HTML special characters, and `<%- value %>` inserts raw HTML for trusted markup only. Rendering user content with `<%-` is stored XSS. Other engines work the same way: Pug uses `#{}` (escaped) and `!{}` (raw), Handlebars `{{}}` and `{{{}}}`. Escape on output, and add a Content Security Policy as defence in depth.
reference: EJS docs: Tags; OWASP: Cross Site Scripting Prevention Cheat Sheet

stem: An Express app calls `app.set('view engine', 'ejs')` and a route calls `res.render('profile', { user })`. With no other view settings, which file does Express render?

options.text: `./profile.ejs` in the folder where the server was started
options.why: Express looks in the views folder, not the project root.

options.text: `views/profile.ejs`, relative to the process's working directory
options.why: The default `views` setting is `process.cwd() + '/views'`.

options.text: `public/profile.html`, served as a static file
options.why: Static files are served by `express.static`, not `res.render`.

options.text: `views/profile.html`, because templates must use the `.html` extension
options.why: The `view engine` setting supplies the extension, here `.ejs`.

explanation: The `views` application setting defaults to `process.cwd() + '/views'`, and the `view engine` setting supplies the default extension. So `res.render('profile')` loads `views/profile.ejs` from the folder the server was started in. Because that depends on the working directory, apps usually set `app.set('views', path.join(__dirname, 'views'))`.
reference: Express docs: Using template engines; app.set (views)

stem:
What does this command print? Type the output.

```bash
node -p "6 * 7"
```
explanation: `node -p` (or `--print`) evaluates the expression and prints the result, while `node -e` evaluates without printing. Both are handy for one-liners in shell scripts, for example `node -p "require('./package.json').version"`. Verified on Node 24.
